rows.title: Sharpness
rows.text: If you are a honeybee, a buff-tailed bumblebee or a common eastern bumblebee, you see roughly a hundredth of the fine detail a human sees, as measured by training bees to tell stripes apart. Nobody has measured how sharply most other bees and wasps see.
rows.note: Left out the giant hornet's estimate and all interommatidial angles, since they are anatomical estimates and the row needs one comparison. The human comparison uses the 30 cycles a degree figure from the brief.

rows.title: Red
rows.text: Honey bees, bumblebees, wool carder bees and hornets each have three kinds of color-sensing cell, which sense ultraviolet, blue and green, and none of them has a cell for red. You very likely have no cell for red either, so red flowers and other red things look dark to you.
rows.note: Left out the single-class records (R15, R18/R19, R20), which look like partial recordings. "Look dark" follows the approved example row and is not stated in any record.

rows.title: Speed
rows.text: If you are a honeybee, you can see a light flicker even when it flashes 200 times a second, where a human stops seeing flicker at about 60. In the bumblebee Bombus hortorum the limit is about 130 flashes a second. Nobody has measured it in wasps, carpenter bees or most other bees.
rows.note: Left out the impulse-response half-widths (R2, R3): they are in milliseconds, not flashes a second, so they give no flicker limit.

rows.title: Ultraviolet
rows.text: Ultraviolet is light that humans cannot see at all. In honeybees, buff-tailed bumblebees, German wasps and several other bees and wasps, recordings from single cells found one kind of color-sensing cell that senses ultraviolet best. Nobody has measured how far into the ultraviolet your own cells reach.
rows.note: Left out peak numbers (no comparison job). Dolichovespula norwegica (R14) lists only blue and green peaks, so I did not claim an ultraviolet cell for all wasps.
